prompt.context: Our client is a large financial services firm with multiple locations around the world. Part of their service offering includes a 24-hour helpline. The client has their call centers in New York and Paris. The client has recently acquired a small firm (Firm B) in order to expand its reach in a particular geography. Firm B provides a subset of the services and has its call center located in the Philippines.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to evaluate its strategy going forward for handling customer calls. In particular, they want us to look into the call center operations. What is your recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client provides a full range of financial services for individuals and small organizations.

clarifying_info.q: How long has Firm B been in operation?
clarifying_info.a: The acquired firm was started 5 years ago and is still run by the original founders.

clarifying_info.q: What are the hiring requirements for call center staff?
clarifying_info.a: New employees are college graduates with basic knowledge of financial services and products. Fluency in English and several European languages is required.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any regulatory constraints on the locations?
clarifying_info.a: It is very difficult to lay off employees in the Paris location, and significant costs will be incurred to do so. The Philippines government encourages investment in the country, so significant tax advantages are possible.

exhibits.title: Call Center Performance – FY2010
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three call centers across calls per year, employee cost per year, overhead cost per year, and number of employees.

framework: Options analysis: (1) No change – maintain all 3 call centers; (2) Close Firm B's Philippines call center and route calls to NY or Paris; (3) Consolidate all calls to a single location (Philippines as lowest cost)
Company / service comparison: compare services offered at each center, product mix handled by each location
Call center performance metrics: cost per call, calls per rep per day, total cost per location
Outsourcing-specific concerns: employment regulations, call quality, language requirements, infrastructure, cultural fit, organizational integration of acquired firm
Financial analysis: total current cost vs. consolidated cost including one-time transition costs; breakeven / payback period

questions.prompt: Calculate key efficiency metrics for each call center: calls per employee per day and cost per call.
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive calls/employee/day and cost/call for each location. New York is most efficient per employee but Philippines is cheapest per call. Paris is least efficient on both dimensions.

math.setup: Assume 200 working days per year. Total cost per location = (employee cost/year × # employees) + overhead. Cost per call = total cost / calls per year.
math.answer: New York: 40 calls/employee/day at $7/call; Paris: 33.3 calls/employee/day at $9/call; Philippines: 20 calls/employee/day at $6/call; Total current cost = $9.6M

questions.prompt: If all calls (1.3M total per year) were consolidated to the Philippines at its current efficiency (20 calls/employee/day), what would the total cost be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the number of employees needed to handle 1.3M calls, then apply Philippines cost structure. Should also note a one-time transition cost of $5M (severance for NY and Paris plus Philippines facility expansion) and compare to current spend.

math.setup: Total calls = 600,000 + 400,000 + 300,000 = 1,300,000. Philippines handles 20 calls/employee/day × 200 days = 4,000 calls/employee/year.
steps: Overhead (scales proportionally from 75 employees at $300K; or given as total with overheads): total including overheads = $6.8M
One-time transition cost = $5M (severance NY + Paris, expanding Philippines facility)
Year 1 total = $6.8M + $5M = $11.8M vs. current $9.6M → not profitable in Year 1; savings in Year 2+ = $9.6M – $6.8M = $2.8M/year
math.answer: Philippines consolidation at current efficiency: ~$6.8M/year ongoing vs. $9.6M current, saving ~$2.8M/year; but $5M one-time cost means Year 1 is not profitable. Payback ~1.8 years, so NOT cost-neutral by Year 2 on its own.

questions.prompt: The CEO requires the solution to be at least cost-neutral by Year 2. What if the Philippines can be trained to match New York's efficiency (40 calls/employee/day)? What would the total cost be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate employees needed at New York efficiency, apply Philippines wages and overhead. Should also raise qualitative concerns about feasibility of achieving this within 3-6 months.

math.setup: Assume best practices transferred in 3-6 months. Philippines at 40 calls/employee/day × 200 days = 8,000 calls/employee/year.
steps: Year 1 net = –$5M (one-time) + $5.75M savings = +$0.75M → cost-neutral by Year 2 is feasible
math.answer: With Philippines at NY efficiency: ~$3.85M/year; annual savings ~$5.75M; covers $5M one-time cost within Year 1, meeting CEO's Year 2 cost-neutral requirement.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and qualitative concerns should the client consider before consolidating call center operations to the Philippines?

categories.name: People / HR
ideas: Ability to hire 163+ qualified college graduates with financial services knowledge and European language fluency in 3-6 months
Knowledge transfer from experienced NY/Paris staff to Philippines team
Regulatory difficulty and significant cost of laying off Paris employees
Severance obligations for New York staff
Cultural integration of acquired firm (still founder-run)

categories.name: Infrastructure & Capacity
ideas: Does Philippines facility have sufficient physical space to roughly double headcount?
Reliability of technology and telecom infrastructure in Philippines
Time zone coverage for 24-hour helpline across geographies

categories.name: Service Quality
ideas: Customers may notice difference in service quality during transition
Language proficiency in European languages for Paris-served customers
Reputational risk if service quality drops; competitors could exploit this to steal customers

categories.name: Organizational / Integration
ideas: Acquired firm is founder-run – culture may clash with large financial firm
Products offered at Philippines may be a subset; full service parity needs to be established
Change management for remaining Philippines staff absorbing much larger volume

categories.name: Regulatory / Tax
ideas: Philippines tax incentives can reduce effective cost further – quantify benefit
Ensure compliance with financial services regulations in all served geographies
Verify no restrictions on routing calls across borders for financial advice

recommendation: Consolidate all call center operations to the Philippines, contingent on achieving New York-level efficiency (40 calls/employee/day) within 3-6 months through best-practice transfer. This yields ~$3.85M/year in ongoing costs vs. $9.6M today, meeting the CEO's Year 2 cost-neutral requirement even after a $5M one-time transition cost.
Alternatively, maintain a hybrid model (keep Paris for European regulatory/language reasons, consolidate NY into Philippines) if laying off Paris staff proves too costly or legally complex.
risks: Capacity and talent risk: hiring 163 qualified, multilingual employees in Philippines within months is aggressive
Service quality risk during transition; reputational damage and customer churn if competitor exploits degraded service
Paris layoff costs are significant and legally complex, potentially eroding savings
Efficiency assumption (matching NY at 40 calls/day) may not be achievable in 3-6 months – if not met, Year 2 cost-neutrality fails
Acquired firm is founder-run; cultural integration and full-service capability build-out add execution risk
next_steps: Assess Philippines facility capacity and infrastructure requirements for 163+ employees
Conduct talent availability study for multilingual college graduates in Philippines labor market
Quantify Paris severance costs and legal timeline to establish true one-time cost
Design best-practice transfer program from New York to Philippines with measurable KPIs
Engage Philippines government on specific tax incentive package to further improve economics
Define customer satisfaction monitoring plan for transition period
